claim: MIG-17 is secreted from cells like muscles to regulate basement membrane proteins.

claim: MIG-17 sustains glia location and morphology during growth.
source: MIG-17 modifies the muscle-derived basement membrane to modulate epidermal-glial crosstalk and sustain glia location and morphology during growth.

claim: Glia position sustains the synaptic pattern established during embryogenesis.

claim: A muscle-epidermis-glia signaling axis sustains synaptic specificity during allometric growth.
source: Our findings uncover a muscle-epidermis-glia signaling axis that sustains synaptic specificity during the organism's allometric growth.
evidence: This is the main conclusion synthesized from multiple lines of genetic, molecular, and cell biological evidence.

claim: Failure to maintain proper synaptic connectivity leads to impaired nervous system function and neurological disorders.
source: Failure to maintain proper synaptic connectivity leads to impaired nervous system function and neurological disorders (Mariano et al., 2018).

claim: Circuit architecture is largely maintained during growth even as tissues change in relative size and position to each other.
source: Remarkably, circuit architecture is largely maintained during growth even as tissues change in relative size and position to each other.

claim: Precise connectivity during development occurs through orchestrated signaling across multiple tissues.
source: These studies indicate that precise connectivity during development occurs through orchestrated signaling across multiple tissues.

claim: Non-neuronal cells are critical in vivo to guide synaptic specificity.
source: While cell-cell recognition and signaling between synaptic partners are pivotal for synaptogenesis, non-neuronal cells are also critical in vivo to guide synaptic specificity (Colón-Ramos, 2009; Margeta and Shen, 2010; Sanes and Yamagata, 2009; Shimozono et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: During development, guidepost cells such as glia instruct synaptic specificity by secreting positional cues to the extracellular matrix.
source: For example, during development, guidepost cells such as glia instruct synaptic specificity by secreting positional cues to the extracellular matrix (ECM) (Ango et al., 2008; Colón-Ramos et al., 2007; Eroglu and Barres, 2010; Molofsky et al., 2014; Shen and Bargmann, 2003; Tsai et al., 2012; Ullian et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Non-cell autonomous mechanisms, mediated through the ECM, can coordinate synaptic connectivity during development in vivo.
source: Therefore, non-cell autonomous mechanisms, mediated through the ECM, can coordinate synaptic connectivity during development in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited literature and established knowledge.

claim: Less is known about the factors required for sustaining the synaptic pattern during post-embryonic growth.

evidence: This represents a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Disrupting ADAMTS metalloproteases and basement membrane proteins impairs the post-embryonic maintenance of the morphology of neuromuscular junctions.
source: In the peripheral nervous system (PNS), disrupting ADAMTS metalloproteases and basement membrane proteins impairs the post-embryonic maintenance of the morphology of neuron-muscle synapses (called neuromuscular junctions, or NMJs) (Cescon et al., 2018; Dear et al., 2016; Heikkinen et al., 2019; Kurshan et al., 2014; Qin et al., 2014; Singhal and Martin, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Basement membrane proteins are important for neuron-neuron synapses in the central nervous system.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Most neuron-neuron synapses in the CNS are not in direct contact with the basement membrane.
source: However, unlike NMJs in the PNS, most neuron-neuron synapses in the CNS are not in direct contact with the basement membrane (Heikkinen et al., 2014; Krishnaswamy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: How the basement membrane sustains CNS neuron-neuron synapses during brain allometric growth remains unknown.
source: How the basement membrane sustains CNS neuron-neuron synapses, particularly during brain allometric growth, remains unknown.
evidence: This represents a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Sustaining the relative synaptic positions during growth is important for sustaining circuit integrity.
source: Sustaining the relative synaptic positions during growth, and therefore embryonically derived synaptic specificity, is important for sustaining circuit integrity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the importance of synaptic connectivity for circuit function.

claim: Allometry is a conserved principle where organs scale in different proportions relative to body size as an animal grows.
source: As an animal grows, organs scale in different proportions relative to body size. This conserved principle is termed 'allometry' (Huxley, 1924; Huxley, 1936).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational literature on allometry.

claim: Neocortical white matter and grey matter scale differently from each other, indicating that specific sub-structures of the brain scale allometrically to total brain size.
source: For relevance to the brain, neocortical white matter and grey matter scale differently from each other, indicating that specific sub-structures of the brain scale allometrically to total brain size (de Jong et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

source: The nematode C. elegans provides a tractable genetic model to examine questions related to sustaining synaptic specificity during growth (Shao et al., 2013).

source: However, ola226 mutants did display a modest but significant defect in VCSC glia morphology, with shorter posterior end-feet in ola226 animals as compared to wild-type animals (length of glia end-feet: 45.52 μm in wild type, 39.79 μm in ola226 p<0.0001. Figure 3E,G).

claim: ola226 mutants displayed a concomitant defect in the position of AIY, as both the neurite and the soma were anteriorly displaced compared to wild type animals.
source: ola226 mutants also displayed a concomitant defect in the position of AIY, as both the neurite and the soma were anteriorly displaced compared to wild type animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images and quantitative measurements.

claim: The anterior displacement of VCSC glia and AIY in ola226 mutants is the opposite phenotype to that observed for cima-1(wy84) mutants, in which these cells are posteriorly displaced.
source: This anterior displacement of VCSC glia and AIY are the opposite phenotype to that observed for cima-1(wy84) mutants, in which these cells are posteriorly displaced (Shao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison of phenotypes supported by data and citations.

claim: In the ola226 mutants, the area of overlap between the glia and AIY was not affected.
source: Interestingly, unlike in cima-1(wy84) mutants, in the ola226 mutants the area of overlap between the glia and AIY was not affected (Figure 3E', H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from microscopy images.

claim: The distribution of presynaptic specializations in ola226 mutants was similar to that seen for wild type.
source: The distribution of presynaptic specializations in these animals was similar to that seen for wild type (Figure 3B', E'), consistent with the importance of glia position in sustaining presynaptic positions.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images showing synaptic patterns.

claim: The relative position between the VCSC glia and the AIY neurons drives presynaptic positions during growth.
source: These phenotypes demonstrate that it is not just glia morphology, glia position or even the position of the AIY neurite in the animal that regulates synaptic allometry. Rather, the relative position between the VCSC glia and the AIY neurons appears to drive presynaptic positions during growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic and cell biological data showing that relative positions matter.

claim: Glia act as guideposts in sustaining the synaptic pattern during post-embryonic growth.
source: Our data underscore the role of glia as guideposts in sustaining the synaptic pattern during post-embryonic growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective findings about glia's role.

claim: The ola226 allele results from a G to A mutation at the end of first exon of the mig-17 gene and alters a conserved glutamic acid residue at position 19 to a lysine.
source: The ola226 allele results from a G to A mutation at the end of first exon of the mig-17 gene and alters a conserved glutamic acid residue at position 19 to a lysine (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by whole genome sequencing data.

claim: mig-17(k113) is a point mutation in the first intron of the gene and is predicted to affect correct splicing.
source: mig-17(k113) is a point mutation in the first intron of the gene and is predicted to affect correct splicing, while the mig-17(k174) allele results from a change in Q111 to a premature stop codon, producing a putative null allele (Figure 4A; Shibata et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by genetic characterization and citations.

claim: The mig-17(k174) allele results from a change in Q111 to a premature stop codon, producing a putative null allele.
source: mig-17(k113) is a point mutation in the first intron of the gene and is predicted to affect correct splicing, while the mig-17(k174) allele results from a change in Q111 to a premature stop codon, producing a putative null allele (Figure 4A; Shibata et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by genetic characterization and citations.

claim: Both k113 and k174 alleles did not display phenotypes in the AIY presynaptic distribution on their own.
source: We found that just like ola226, both k113 and k174 alleles did not display phenotypes in the AIY presynaptic distribution on their own (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), yet robustly suppressed the ectopic presynaptic sites in cima-1(wy84) mutants (91.9% of animals displayed ectopic presynaptic sites in cima-1(wy84), 62.3% in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(k113), 29.9% in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(k174) and 45.7% in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226), p<0.0001 for all double mutants as compared to cima-1(wy84); Figure 4B–F,H).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images showing normal synaptic patterns.

claim: k113 and k174 alleles robustly suppressed the ectopic presynaptic sites in cima-1(wy84) mutants.
source: We found that just like ola226, both k113 and k174 alleles did not display phenotypes in the AIY presynaptic distribution on their own (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), yet robustly suppressed the ectopic presynaptic sites in cima-1(wy84) mutants (91.9% of animals displayed ectopic presynaptic sites in cima-1(wy84), 62.3% in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(k113), 29.9% in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(k174) and 45.7% in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226), p<0.0001 for all double mutants as compared to cima-1(wy84); Figure 4B–F,H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from microscopy images.

claim: 91.9% of cima-1(wy84) animals displayed ectopic presynaptic sites, 62.3% in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(k113), 29.9% in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(k174) and 45.7% in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226) (p<0.0001 for all double mutants as compared to cima-1(wy84)).
source: We found that just like ola226, both k113 and k174 alleles did not display phenotypes in the AIY presynaptic distribution on their own (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), yet robustly suppressed the ectopic presynaptic sites in cima-1(wy84) mutants (91.9% of animals displayed ectopic presynaptic sites in cima-1(wy84), 62.3% in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(k113), 29.9% in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(k174) and 45.7% in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226), p<0.0001 for all double mutants as compared to cima-1(wy84); Figure 4B–F,H).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the experiments.

claim: Introducing a wild-type copy of the mig-17 genomic sequence results in robust rescue of the ola226 phenotype in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226) double mutants.
source: Importantly, introducing a wild-type copy of the mig-17 genomic sequence results in robust rescue of the ola226 phenotype in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226) double mutants (45.70% of animals displayed ectopic synapses in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226) and 78.04% in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226);Pmig-17::mig-17(genomic), p<0.0001; Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from rescue experiments.

claim: 45.70% of cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226) animals displayed ectopic synapses compared to 78.04% in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226);Pmig-17::mig-17(genomic) (p<0.0001).
source: Importantly, introducing a wild-type copy of the mig-17 genomic sequence results in robust rescue of the ola226 phenotype in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226) double mutants (45.70% of animals displayed ectopic synapses in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226) and 78.04% in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226);Pmig-17::mig-17(genomic), p<0.0001; Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This is quantitative data from rescue experiments.

claim: ola226 is a recessive loss-of-function allele of mig-17 which suppresses cima-1(wy84) defects in synaptic allometry by affecting glia positions during growth.
source: Together our findings indicate that ola226 is a recessive loss-of-function allele of mig-17 which suppresses cima-1(wy84) defects in synaptic allometry by affecting glia positions during growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic characterization and rescue experiments.

claim: MIG-17 is an ADAMTS metalloprotease best known for its post-embryonic roles in regulating distal tip cell migration during gonad development and pharyngeal size and shape during growth.
source: MIG-17 is an ADAMTS metalloprotease best known for its post-embryonic roles in regulating distal tip cell migration during gonad development (Nishiwaki, 1999) and pharyngeal size and shape during growth (Shibata et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ADAMTS proteins have been shown to regulate the basement membrane to maintain synaptic morphology at neuromuscular junctions.
source: ADAMTS proteins have also been shown to regulate the basement membrane to maintain synaptic morphology at neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) (Kurshan et al., 2014; Qin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The basement membrane is not in direct contact with synapses in the nerve ring, including the AIY synapses.
source: Unlike the NMJs, the basement membrane is not in direct contact with synapses in the nerve ring, including the AIY synapses (White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and anatomical observations.

claim: The basement membrane cannot signal directly to AIY synapses as it does to the NMJs.
source: Therefore, the basement membrane cannot signal directly to AIY synapses as it does to the NMJs (Kurshan et al., 2014; Qin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical relationship and citations.

claim: MIG-17 modulates synaptic allometry in AIY through the modulation of VCSC glia position and morphology.
source: Instead, our collective findings suggest that MIG-17 modulates synaptic allometry in AIY through the modulation of VCSC glia position and morphology.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic and cell biological data.

claim: A mig-17 transcriptional GFP reporter was robustly expressed by body wall muscles.
source: We found that a mig-17 transcriptional GFP reporter was robustly expressed by body wall muscles as colabeled by Pmyo-3::mCherry (Figure 5A–A''' and consistent with Nishiwaki et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images showing reporter expression.

claim: In the head region, the mig-17 reporter was detected in the nervous system.
source: We also observed that in the head region, the reporter was detected in the nervous system (Figure 5B–B''').
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images showing reporter expression.

claim: MIG-17 expression was not detected in VCSC glial cells or in epidermal cells.
source: We did not detect expression of MIG-17 in VCSC glial cells or in epidermal cells, where the MIG-17 genetic interactors CIMA-1 and EGL-15/FGFR are expressed (Figure 5C–D'''; Shao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images showing lack of reporter expression in these cells.

claim: Robust rescue of the cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226) phenotype was observed when mig-17 was expressed either in body wall muscles or in the nervous system.
source: We found robust rescue of the cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226) phenotype when mig-17 was expressed either in body wall muscles or in the nervous system (Figure 5E), consistent with MIG-17 being a secreted ADAMTS protease.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from rescue experiments.

claim: MIG-17 is a secreted ADAMTS protease.
source: We found robust rescue of the cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226) phenotype when mig-17 was expressed either in body wall muscles or in the nervous system (Figure 5E), consistent with MIG-17 being a secreted ADAMTS protease.
evidence: This is supported by the rescue experiments and established knowledge about ADAMTS proteases.

claim: Expression of MIG-17 from a number of different cell-specific promoters, including glia and epidermal cells, all resulted in rescue.
source: Indeed, expression of MIG-17 from a number of different cell-specific promoters, including glia and epidermal cells in which we did not detect expression, all resulted in rescue (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from rescue experiments.

claim: Secreted MIG-17 modulates glia morphology and synaptic allometry.
source: Together, our findings suggest that secreted MIG-17 modulates glia morphology and synaptic allometry.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression and rescue data.

claim: The engineered mig-17(shc8) allele behaved like other mig-17 loss-of-function alleles and suppressed ectopic synapses in cima-1(wy84) mutant animals.
source: We observed that our engineered mig-17(shc8) allele behaved like other mig-17 loss-of-function alleles and suppressed ectopic synapses in cima-1(wy84) mutant animals (91.91% of animals displayed ectopic synapses in cima-1(wy84) vs 57.49% in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(shc8), p<0.0001, Figure 6B–E,H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from experiments with the engineered allele.

claim: 91.91% of cima-1(wy84) animals displayed ectopic synapses compared to 57.49% in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(shc8) (p<0.0001).
source: We observed that our engineered mig-17(shc8) allele behaved like other mig-17 loss-of-function alleles and suppressed ectopic synapses in cima-1(wy84) mutant animals (91.91% of animals displayed ectopic synapses in cima-1(wy84) vs 57.49% in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(shc8), p<0.0001, Figure 6B–E,H).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the experiments.

claim: A transgene with the E303A (mig-17(E303A)) lesion is incapable of rescuing the mig-17-induced suppression in mig-17(ola226);cima-1(wy84) mutants.
source: Consistent with this result, we also found that a transgene with the E303A (mig-17(E303A)) lesion is incapable of rescuing the mig-17-induced suppression in mig-17(ola226);cima-1(wy84) mutants (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from rescue experiments.

claim: MIG-17 metalloprotease enzymatic activity is required for promoting the formation of ectopic synapses in cima-1(wy84) mutants.
source: These findings indicate that MIG-17 metalloprotease enzymatic activity is required for promoting the formation of ectopic synapses in cima-1(wy84) mutants, and are consistent with a model whereby MIG-17 remodels the basement membrane to modulate synaptic allometry during growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data from the catalytic mutant experiments.

claim: MIG-17 remodels the basement membrane to modulate synaptic allometry during growth.
source: These findings indicate that MIG-17 metalloprotease enzymatic activity is required for promoting the formation of ectopic synapses in cima-1(wy84) mutants, and are consistent with a model whereby MIG-17 remodels the basement membrane to modulate synaptic allometry during growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enzymatic activity requirement and known functions of ADAMTS proteases.

claim: Significant and reproducible differences in the protein levels of basement membrane components were observed for mig-17(ola226) mutants compared to wild type.
source: Consistent with the known importance of MIG-17 in remodeling the basement membrane in other biological contexts (Kim and Nishiwaki, 2015), we observed significant and reproducible differences in the protein levels of basement membrane components for mig-17(ola226) mutants compared to wild type, including EMB-9/Collagen IV α1 chain, LET-2/Collagen IV α2 chain, OST-1/Sparc, UNC-52/Perlecan, NID-1/nidogen, EPI-1/laminin-α, LAM-1/laminin-β, and LAM-2/laminin-γ (Figure 7A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic mass spectrometry data.

claim: Basement membrane components upregulated in mig-17(ola226) mutants include EMB-9/Collagen IV α1 chain, LET-2/Collagen IV α2 chain, OST-1/Sparc, UNC-52/Perlecan, NID-1/nidogen, EPI-1/laminin-α, LAM-1/laminin-β, and LAM-2/laminin-γ.
source: Consistent with the known importance of MIG-17 in remodeling the basement membrane in other biological contexts (Kim and Nishiwaki, 2015), we observed significant and reproducible differences in the protein levels of basement membrane components for mig-17(ola226) mutants compared to wild type, including EMB-9/Collagen IV α1 chain, LET-2/Collagen IV α2 chain, OST-1/Sparc, UNC-52/Perlecan, NID-1/nidogen, EPI-1/laminin-α, LAM-1/laminin-β, and LAM-2/laminin-γ (Figure 7A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic mass spectrometry data.

claim: EMB-9/Collagen IV α1 is a core component of the basement membrane regulated by ADAMTS proteins.
source: EMB-9/Collagen IV α1 is a core component of the basement membrane regulated by ADAMTS proteins (Graham et al., 1997; Guo et al., 1991; Sibley et al., 1993) and plays important roles in post-embryonic neuromuscular junction morphology (Kurshan et al., 2014; Qin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EMB-9/Collagen IV α1 plays important roles in post-embryonic neuromuscular junction morphology.
source: EMB-9/Collagen IV α1 is a core component of the basement membrane regulated by ADAMTS proteins (Graham et al., 1997; Guo et al., 1991; Sibley et al., 1993) and plays important roles in post-embryonic neuromuscular junction morphology (Kurshan et al., 2014; Qin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EMB-9 null alleles are embryonic lethal.
source: Since EMB-9 null alleles are embryonic lethal (Guo et al., 1991; Gupta et al., 1997), we used neomorphic or hypomorphic missense alleles that disrupt NMJ morphology and are predicted to produce overabundant or disorganized collagen (Gotenstein et al., 2018; Gupta et al., 1997; Kubota et al., 2012; Kurshan et al., 2014; Qin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: No detectable defects in the AIY presynaptic site distribution or morphology were observed in emb-9(xd51) or emb-9(b189) mutants.
source: We did not observe detectable defects in the AIY presynaptic site distribution or morphology in emb-9(xd51) or emb-9(b189) mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images and quantitative data.

claim: EMB-9/Collagen IV can become overabundant or disorganized in ADAMTs mutants.
source: Interestingly, EMB-9/Collagen IV can also become overabundant or disorganized in ADAMTs mutants (Kim and Nishiwaki, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Neomorphic and hypomorphic emb-9 alleles significantly suppressed the ectopic presynaptic sites in cima-1(wy84) mutant animals.
source: Indeed, we observed that neomorphic and hypomorphic emb-9 alleles significantly suppressed the ectopic presynaptic sites in cima-1(wy84) mutant animals, although the penetrance of the suppression phenotype varied by the specific allele (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from genetic experiments.

claim: While emb-9 alleles do not affect the morphology of AIY presynaptic sites, they significantly suppress the synaptic allometry defects for cima-1 mutants.
source: Therefore, while the emb-9 alleles do not affect the morphology of AIY presynaptic sites (as they do for NMJ synapses), they significantly suppress the synaptic allometry defects for cima-1 mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of phenotypes.

claim: cima-1 mutants are suppressed both by mig-17 and the neomorphic and hypomorphic emb-9 alleles because the material properties of the basement membrane are altered.
source: We hypothesized that cima-1 mutants are suppressed both by mig-17 and the neomorphic and hypomorphic emb-9 alleles because in these mutants the material properties of the basement membrane are altered.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Altered basement membrane properties would prevent the movement of glia during growth and suppress the ectopic contacts between glia and AIY seen for cima-1 mutants.
source: This, in turn, would prevent the movement of glia during growth and suppress the ectopic contacts between glia and AIY seen for cima-1 mutants.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Loss-of-function alleles of unc-52/Perlecan significantly suppressed the ectopic presynaptic sites observed in cima-1(wy84) mutants.
source: Consistent with our model, loss-of-function alleles of unc-52/Perlecan, which is known to functionally antagonize EMB-9/Collagen IV (Qin et al., 2014), significantly suppressed the ectopic presynaptic sites observed in cima-1(wy84) mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from genetic experiments.

claim: unc-52/Perlecan is known to functionally antagonize EMB-9/Collagen IV.
source: Consistent with our model, loss-of-function alleles of unc-52/Perlecan, which is known to functionally antagonize EMB-9/Collagen IV (Qin et al., 2014), significantly suppressed the ectopic presynaptic sites observed in cima-1(wy84) mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The gain-of-function fbl-1(k201) allele suppressed the ectopic presynaptic sites observed in cima-1(wy84) mutants.
source: Similarly, the gain-of-function fbl-1(k201) allele (Kubota et al., 2004), which is predicted to cause an overabundance of EMB-9 (Kubota et al., 2012), also suppressed the ectopic presynaptic sites observed in cima-1(wy84) mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from genetic experiments.

claim: The gain-of-function fbl-1(k201) allele is predicted to cause an overabundance of EMB-9.
source: Similarly, the gain-of-function fbl-1(k201) allele (Kubota et al., 2004), which is predicted to cause an overabundance of EMB-9 (Kubota et al., 2012), also suppressed the ectopic presynaptic sites observed in cima-1(wy84) mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The levels of suppression in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226);fbl-1(k201) are similar to those seen in either cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226) or in cima-1(wy84);fbl-1(k201) mutants.
source: We also determined that the levels of suppression in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226);fbl-1(k201) are similar to those seen in either cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226) or in cima-1(wy84);fbl-1(k201) mutants, consistent with mig-17 and fbl-1 genetically acting in the same pathway (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from genetic experiments.

claim: mig-17 and fbl-1 genetically act in the same pathway.
source: We also determined that the levels of suppression in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226);fbl-1(k201) are similar to those seen in either cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226) or in cima-1(wy84);fbl-1(k201) mutants, consistent with mig-17 and fbl-1 genetically acting in the same pathway (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic epistasis data.

claim: Lesions resulting in defects in the basement membrane might prevent the repositioning of glia that gives rise to the ectopic presynaptic sites in cima-1(wy84) mutants.
source: Their shared ability to suppress cima-1(wy84) mutants suggests that lesions resulting in defects in the basement membrane might prevent the repositioning of glia that gives rise to the ectopic presynaptic sites in cima-1(wy84) mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective genetic data.

claim: Both MIG-17 and EMB-9 localize in the head-region to a pattern reminiscent of the extracellular matrix proximal to the pharynx bulb.
source: We observed that both MIG-17 and EMB-9 localize in the head-region to a pattern reminiscent of the extracellular matrix proximal to the pharynx bulb (Ihara et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images of fluorescent reporters.

claim: The levels of MIG-17 and EMB-9 were regulated during post-embryonic growth.
source: We also determined that the levels of MIG-17 and EMB-9 were regulated during post-embryonic growth.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements of fluorescent reporters at different stages.

claim: MIG-17 protein levels were detectable in larva stage one through larva stage 4, but became undetectable upon reaching the adult stage.
source: MIG-17 protein levels were detectable in larva stage one through larva stage 4, but became undetectable upon reaching the adult stage (Figure 7C–G, these results are consistent with previous in situ and western blot studies; Ihara and Nishiwaki, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements of fluorescent reporters and citations.

claim: EMB-9 protein levels increased as animals progress through the larval stages, achieving maximal expression in the adult stage.
source: Conversely, EMB-9 protein levels increased as animals progress through the larval stages, achieving maximal expression in the adult stage (Figure 7H–L).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements of fluorescent reporters.

claim: During post-embryonic growth, high protein levels of MIG-17 correlate with low protein levels of EMB-9.
source: Therefore, during post-embryonic growth, high protein levels of MIG-17 correlate with low protein levels of EMB-9.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal expression patterns observed.

claim: MIG-17 regulates EMB-9 and basement membrane properties directly or indirectly.
source: The in vivo characterization of the protein levels of MIG-17 and EMB-9 are consistent with our proteomic results, and suggest that, directly or indirectly, MIG-17 regulates EMB-9 and basement membrane properties.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic and expression data.

claim: EMB-9::mCherry levels in mig-17(ola226) mutant animals were upregulated as compared to wild type.
source: Consistent with these findings, EMB-9::mCherry levels in mig-17(ola226) mutant animals were upregulated as compared to wild type (Figure 7M–Q).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements of fluorescent reporters.

claim: The increase in EMB-9 levels observed for mig-17(ola226) mutant was suppressed in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226) double mutants.
source: Interestingly, this increase in EMB-9 levels observed for mig-17(ola226) mutant was suppressed in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226) double mutants, suggesting the existence of other cima-1-dependent mechanisms that modulate EMB-9 levels in the absence of MIG-17 (Figure 7P and Q).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements of fluorescent reporters.

claim: There exist other cima-1-dependent mechanisms that modulate EMB-9 levels in the absence of MIG-17.
source: Interestingly, this increase in EMB-9 levels observed for mig-17(ola226) mutant was suppressed in cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226) double mutants, suggesting the existence of other cima-1-dependent mechanisms that modulate EMB-9 levels in the absence of MIG-17 (Figure 7P and Q).
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic data.

claim: MIG-17 regulates EMB-9 and basement membrane properties to modulate synaptic allometry during post-embryonic growth.
source: Importantly, our observations indicate that MIG-17 regulates EMB-9 and basement membrane properties to modulate synaptic allometry during post-embryonic growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective findings.

claim: Secreted metalloprotease MIG-17, whose levels are regulated during post-embryonic growth, dynamically regulates the muscle-derived basement membrane.
source: Together, our findings support a model in which secreted metalloprotease MIG-17, whose levels are regulated during post-embryonic growth, dynamically regulates the muscle-derived basement membrane.
evidence: This is a model synthesized from the collective findings.

claim: Through regulation of the basement membrane, MIG-17 modulates cima-1-dependent epidermal-glial crosstalk to regulate glia position and morphology and sustain synaptic allometry during growth.
source: Through regulation of the basement membrane, MIG-17 modulates cima-1-dependent epidermal-glial crosstalk to regulate glia position and morphology and sustain synaptic allometry during growth.
evidence: This is a model synthesized from the collective findings.

claim: CIMA-1 modulates epidermal-glial cell adhesion via regulation of EGL-15/FGFR ectodomain which acts as an extracellular adhesion factor.
source: CIMA-1 modulates epidermal-glial cell adhesion via regulation of EGL-15/FGFR ectodomain which acts, not in its canonical signaling role, but as an extracellular adhesion factor (Bülow et al., 2004; Shao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: CIMA-1 is required to regulate EGL-15(5A)/FGFR protein levels.
source: Consistent with this model, CIMA-1 is required to regulate EGL-15(5A)/FGFR protein levels, and overexpression of the EGL-15(5A)/FGFR ectodomain in wild-type animals phenocopied cima-1 mutants (Shao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Overexpression of the EGL-15(5A)/FGFR ectodomain in wild-type animals phenocopied cima-1 mutants.
source: Consistent with this model, CIMA-1 is required to regulate EGL-15(5A)/FGFR protein levels, and overexpression of the EGL-15(5A)/FGFR ectodomain in wild-type animals phenocopied cima-1 mutants (Shao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: cima-1(wy84);egl-15(n484) double mutants, cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226) double mutants and cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226);egl-15(n484) triple mutants all suppressed the cima-1(wy84) phenotype of ectopic presynaptic sites in a similar manner.
source: We determined that cima-1(wy84);egl-15(n484) double mutants, cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226) double mutants and cima-1(wy84);mig-17(ola226);egl-15(n484) triple mutants all suppressed the cima-1(wy84) phenotype of ectopic presynaptic sites in a similar manner (Figure 8A–D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from genetic experiments.

claim: Alleles for mig-17 and egl-15 similarly suppress the cima-1 phenotype, and are incapable of enhancing each other's effect on the suppression of cima-1.
source: Importantly, these findings indicate that alleles for mig-17 and egl-15 similarly suppress the cima-1 phenotype, and are incapable of enhancing each other's effect on the suppression of cima-1, consistent with them acting in different tissues, but in similar genetic pathways to suppress cima-1 mutant defects in synaptic allometry.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic epistasis data.

claim: mig-17 and egl-15 act in different tissues, but in similar genetic pathways to suppress cima-1 mutant defects in synaptic allometry.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic and cell biological data.
